title: The State of Grid-Scale Energy Storage
subtitle: How falling battery costs are rewiring the economics of renewable power
author: Prepared for the 2026 Energy Transition Briefing
topic_prompt: grid-scale energy storage, renewable energy economics
abstract: Global grid-scale battery deployments reached 92 GW of cumulative capacity in 2025, a 41% year-on-year jump, while average pack prices fell below $95/kWh for the first time. This briefing maps where that capacity landed, what it did to wholesale power markets, and which storage technologies will define the next build-out cycle.
conclusion: Storage is no longer the bottleneck of the energy transition — financing and interconnection queues are. The developers who win the next five years will be the ones who treat batteries as market instruments, not infrastructure.

sections.heading: The State of Grid-Scale Energy Storage
sections.subtitle: How falling battery costs are rewiring the economics of renewable power
sections.tagline: Bauhaus Data | 92 GW installed. $95/kWh. The grid will never be the same.
sections.callout: Storage stopped being a technology bet in 2025. It became a market position.
sections.speaker_notes: Open with the headline: storage crossed from pilot economics to portfolio economics in a single year. This deck shows where, why, and what happens next.

sections.heading: Three numbers that changed the market
sections.body: The 2025 build-out was not incremental — it doubled the pace of every prior year. Cumulative grid-scale capacity hit 92 GW globally, with China and the United States accounting for 71% of additions. Average lithium-iron-phosphate pack prices broke the $95/kWh floor analysts once called impossible before 2030, and four-hour systems began clearing capacity auctions against gas peakers outright.

sections.speaker_notes: Anchor the audience in three numbers: 92 gigawatts installed, sub-95-dollar packs, and a two-country race. Everything later builds on these.

sections.heading: Batteries vs. gas peakers
sections.body: Levelized cost comparisons flipped in 2025 for the first time in mid-merit applications. A four-hour battery now delivers firm evening capacity at $118/MWh against $142/MWh for a new-build gas peaker in ERCOT-like markets, before any tax credit. The gap widens to 34% with investment credits applied.
left_points: Firm evening capacity at $118/MWh levelized in high-solar markets, falling roughly 8% per year
Captures arbitrage plus ancillary revenue stacks worth $28-45/kW-year on top of capacity payments
Deploys in 14-20 months from notice to commercial operation
right_points: Firm capacity at $142/MWh levelized and rising with turbine backlogs stretching to 2029
Single revenue stream exposed to fuel basis risk and tightening emissions rules
Development timelines of 3-5 years including air permits and gas interconnection
sections.speaker_notes: Walk the cost crossover: batteries beat new peakers on levelized cost in 2025. Note the turbine supply backlog pushing gas timelines out to 2029.

sections.heading: What a 1 GWh site actually looks like
sections.body: The Edwards & Sanborn complex in Kern County set the template: 4,600 containerized packs across 4.5 square kilometres, co-located with 875 MW of solar and a single 500 kV interconnection. Co-location cut interconnection cost per megawatt by 38% versus standalone siting, and shared inverters lifted round-trip efficiency to 87%. The industry copied it — 62% of 2025 US additions were solar-paired.
highlights: Co-location cuts interconnection cost per MW by 38%
Shared inverters lift round-trip efficiency to 87%
62% of 2025 US additions were solar-paired hybrids
sections.image_keyword: aerial view of large solar farm with battery storage containers in desert
sections.speaker_notes: Use the Edwards and Sanborn example to make the scale physical: 4,600 containers, one interconnection point. Co-location is now the default architecture.

sections.heading: The duck curve is being paid to flatten
sections.body: California's evening ramp — once the poster child of renewable intermittency — shrank 31% in 2025 as 11.2 GW of state storage shifted solar into the peak. Evening price spikes above $200/MWh fell from 118 hours in 2022 to 22 hours in 2025, and storage captured an average spread of $61/MWh doing it.

sections.heading: Four eras of storage economics
sections.body: Each era compressed faster than the last. What took pumped hydro four decades took lithium-ion cell economics one.

steps.desc: Utility demonstrations under 10 MW prove round-trip viability; costs above $600/kWh.
Frequency-regulation markets in PJM and UK fund the first merchant fleets.
Four-hour systems win capacity auctions; solar-paired hybrids become the default.
Sub-$95/kWh packs make pure arbitrage bankable without subsidy in high-spread markets.

sections.speaker_notes: Compress twelve years into four eras. The point: each business model funded the cost curve that enabled the next one.

sections.heading: The trader's view
sections.callout: We stopped modelling batteries as assets with a depreciation schedule and started modelling them as options on volatility. That single change re-priced our entire pipeline.
sections.attribution: — Head of Power Trading, European utility, January 2026
highlights: Volatility-based valuation lifted project NPVs 22% on average
Two-hour systems repriced below four-hour for the first time
Toll agreements now cover 58% of new European capacity
sections.speaker_notes: Let the quote breathe — it captures the mental shift from infrastructure to instrument. The three side cards quantify what that reframing did.

sections.heading: What breaks the pattern
sections.body: Three forces could bend the curve again before 2030: sodium-ion cells entering mass production at a projected $56/kWh, iron-air pilots proving 100-hour duration at utility scale, and interconnection reform unlocking the 2.6 TW of storage-hybrid projects stuck in US queues.
statements: Sodium-ion moves the floor: $56/kWh cells make storage a commodity, not a supply chain race.
100-hour iron-air turns storage from a peaker replacement into a transmission replacement.
The queue is the new OPEC: 2.6 TW of projects wait on paperwork, not physics.
sections.speaker_notes: Close the analysis section by naming the three discontinuities to watch: sodium-ion pricing, long-duration chemistry, and interconnection reform.

sections.heading: Four moves for the next 24 months
sections.body: The window where storage knowledge is a competitive edge is closing. These four positions matter most before 2028.

tiles.label: SITE
tiles.value: Lock interconnection positions now — queue time, not capex, is the scarcest asset in the market.

tiles.label: STACK
tiles.value: Underwrite on revenue stacks, not single streams; arbitrage-only models leave 30% of value uncaptured.

tiles.label: SIZE
tiles.value: Follow the spread: two-hour systems now clear better risk-adjusted returns in half of US markets.

tiles.label: SCAN
tiles.value: Track sodium-ion factory commissioning as the leading indicator of the next price break.

sections.speaker_notes: End the body with actions, not observations: site control, revenue stacking, right-sizing duration, and watching the sodium-ion supply chain.

sections.heading: The grid is becoming a market with a memory
sections.body: Every gigawatt of storage added makes electricity prices smoother, evening capacity cheaper, and the next gigawatt easier to finance. That feedback loop — not any single technology — is the story of this decade.
sections.cta: Take one project through volatility-based valuation this quarter.
